#### Proposition 5.9.

$c_{\alpha,w}=\#X_{\alpha,w}$ .

#### Proof.

Iterating (23),

$$ {\mathfrak{S}}_{w}=\sum_{\text{vexillary }v\in S_{\infty}}\sum_{S\in{\sf Trans}(w,v)}x^{{\sf delwt}(S)}{\mathfrak{S}}_{v}. $$

Hence

$$ c_{\alpha,w}=\sum_{\text{vexillary }v\in S_{\infty}}\sum_{S\in{\sf Trans}(w,v)}[x^{\alpha}]x^{{\sf delwt}(S)}{\mathfrak{S}}_{v}. $$

The result then follows from by (21), (22), and (25) combined.∎

#### Proposition 5.10 (cf. [8]).

Let ${\sf code}(w)=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{L})$ . Suppose $D(w^{\prime})$ is obtained from $D(w)$ using move (T.1) and $D(w^{\prime\prime})$ is obtained from $D(w)$ with move (T.2) for a pivot in row $i$ . There is an $O(L^{2})$ -time algorithm to compute

- (I) ${\sf code}(w^{\prime})=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r-1},c_{r}-1,c_{r+1},\ldots,c_{L})$ and

- (II) ${\sf code}(w^{\prime\prime})=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{i-1},c_{i}+b,c_{i+1},\ldots,c_{r-1},c_{r}-b,c_{r+1},\ldots,c_{L})$ , for some $b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 3.2, determine $\mathbf{z}_{w}:=(r,c)$ in $O(L^{2})$ -time.

For (I), $D(w^{\prime})$ is obtained from $D(w)$ by deleting $\mathbf{z}_{w}$ ; so the expression in (I) is clear.

For (II), using Proposition 3.1, we can find $\mathbf{x}=(i,w(i))$ , in $O(L^{2})$ -time; this is our (T.2) pivot. Notice that row $r$ of $D(w)\cap{\mathcal{R}}$ is nonempty (it contains $\mathbf{z}_{w}=(r,c)$ ); let $b$ be the number of boxes in this row. It is straightforward from the graphical description of ${\mathcal{R}}$ in terms of Rothe diagrams that each row of $D(w)\cap{\mathcal{R}}$ either has zero boxes or $b>0$ boxes. Moreover, the $d$ -th box (say, from the left) of each row are in the same column.

Suppose $j_{1},\ldots,j_{m}\in[i+1,r]$ index the rows where $D(w)\cap{\mathcal{R}}\neq\emptyset$ (and thus has $b$ boxes). (T.2) moves the $b$ boxes of $j_{1}$ to row $i$ and moves the $b$ boxes of $j_{q}$ to row $j_{q-1}$ for $q=2,\ldots,m$ . As explained above $j_{m}=r$ , so (T.2) moves no boxes into row $r$ . Thus row $r$ of $D(w^{\prime\prime})\cap{\mathcal{R}}$ has zero boxes.

It remains to compute $b$ in $O(L^{2})$ -time. Using Proposition 3.1 compute, in $O(L^{2})$ -time,

$$ m:=\#\{h<r\ :\ w(h)<w(i)\}. $$

Clearly $b=c_{r}-[(w(i)-1)-m]$ . ∎

Let $s_{t}=(x_{r},m_{t})$ , as in (X.1), be a valid (multi)-deletion move on $u\in\mathcal{T}(w)$ . Let $u^{\langle m\rangle}\in\mathcal{T}(w)$ be defined by $u\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x_{k}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bullet\cdots\bullet\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x_{k}}}{{\longrightarrow}}u^{\langle m_{t}\rangle}$ ( $m_{t}$ -times).

#### Proposition 5.11.

Suppose $u\in\mathcal{T}(w)$ where ${\sf code}(u)=({\widetilde{c}}_{1},\ldots,{\widetilde{c}}_{L^{\prime}})$ . Let $s_{t}=(x_{k},m_{t})$ or $s_{t}=i$ be as in (X.1). Given input ${\sf code}(u)$ and $s_{t}$ , there is an $O(L^{2})$ algorithm to respectively determine if $u\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x_{k}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bullet\cdots\bullet\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x_{k}}}{{\longrightarrow}}u^{\langle m_{t}\rangle}$ ( $m_{t}$ -times) or $u\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\longrightarrow}}u^{\prime\prime}$ occurs in ${\mathcal{T}}(w)$ and (if yes) to compute

- • ${\sf code}(u^{\langle m_{t}\rangle})$ in the case $s_{t}=(x_{k},m_{t})$ (a multi-deletion move (T.1)), or

- • ${\sf code}(u^{\prime\prime})$ in the case $s_{t}=i$ (a march move (T.2)).

#### Proof.

By Proposition 5.10, $L^{\prime}\leq L$ . Thus in our run-time analysis, we replace $L^{\prime}$ by $L$ .

Proposition 3.2 finds $\mathbf{z}_{u}:=(r,c)$ (or determines it does not exist) in $O(L^{2})$ -time. If $\mathbf{z}_{u}$ does not exist then $u$ is dominant and thus vexillary; output $s_{t}$ is invalid. Thus we assume henceforth that $\mathbf{z}_{u}$ exists.

Case 1: ( $s_{t}=(x_{k},m_{t})$ .) Proposition 3.1 finds $u(1),\ldots,u(L^{\prime})$ in $O(L^{2})$ -time. Determine (taking $O(L^{2})$ time) if

$$ c_{r}-\left(\left(\min_{i\in[r]}{u(i)}\right)-1\right)\geq m_{t}, $$

holds. We claim that $s_{t}$ is valid if and only if (26) holds and $k=r$ . Indeed, observe

$$ \#\{\text{boxes in row $r$ of ${\sf Dom}(u)$}\}=\left(\min_{i\in[r]}{u(i)}\right)-1. $$

Thus, (26) is equivalent to the existence of $m_{t}$ boxes in row $r$ of $D(u)\smallsetminus{\sf Dom}(u)$ . By (T.1), if $k=r$ this is equivalent to being able to apply $\bullet\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x_{r}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bullet$ successively $m_{t}$ -times.

Finally, if $s_{t}$ is valid, by $m_{t}$ applications of Proposition 5.10 (I),

$$ {\sf code}(u^{\langle m_{t}\rangle})=({\widetilde{c}}_{1},\ldots,{\widetilde{c}}_{r-1},{\widetilde{c}}_{r}-m_{t},{\widetilde{c}}_{r+1},\ldots,{\widetilde{c}}_{L^{\prime}}). $$

Hence we can output (28) in $O(L^{2})$ -time.

Case 2: ( $s_{t}=i$ .) By Proposition 3.1, determine $u(1),\ldots,u(L^{\prime})$ from ${\sf code}(u)$ in $O(L^{2})$ -time. In particular this computes $\mathbf{x}:=(i,u(i))$ in $O(L^{2})$ -time. To decide if $s_{t}$ is valid we must determine if $\mathbf{x}\in{\sf Piv}(\mathbf{z}_{u})$ . To do this, first calculate (in $O(L)$ -time)

$$ u_{NW}(\mathbf{z}_{u}):=\{(j,u(j))\ :\ j<r,u(j)<c\}. $$

By definition,

$$ {\sf Piv}(\mathbf{z}_{u})=\{(j,u(j))\in u_{NW}(\mathbf{z}_{u})\ :\ \nexists(h,u(h))\in u_{NW}(\mathbf{z}_{u})\mbox{ with }h>j,u(h)>u(j)\}. $$

${\sf Piv}(\mathbf{z}_{u})$ takes $O(L)$ -time to compute since $\#u_{NW}(\mathbf{z}_{u})\leq r-1\leq L-1$ . Hence we check if $\mathbf{x}\in{\sf Piv}(\mathbf{z}_{u})$ in $O(L)$ -time. If this is false, we output a rejection. Otherwise, Proposition 5.10 outputs ${\sf code}(u^{\prime\prime})$ in $O(L^{2})$ -time. ∎

#### Proposition 5.12.

If $S=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{h})\in{\sf Trans}(w,v)$ then $h\leq L^{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $w:=w_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}w_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\ldots\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s_{h}}}{{\longrightarrow}}w_{h}=v$ be the path in $\mathcal{T}(w)$ associated to $S$ . By (T.1) and (T.2), ${\mathbf{z}}_{w_{t+1}}$ is weakly northwest of ${\mathbf{z}}_{w_{t}}$ . Hence, for any fixed $r$ , those $t\in[0,h-1]$ with $\mathbf{z}_{w_{t}}$ in row $r$ form an interval $I^{(r)}\subseteq[0,h-1]$ . Since $1\leq r\leq L$ , it suffices to prove

$$ \#I^{(r)}\leq 2(r-1). $$

By (X.1) the transition moves acting on row $r$ alternate between multi-(T.1) moves $(x_{r},m_{t})$ and (T.2) moves. Thus to show (29), it is enough to prove

$$ \#\{t\in I^{(r)}:w_{t-1}\to w_{t}\text{ \ is a (T.2) move}\}\leq r-1. $$

Consider a march move $i$ with $\mathbf{z}_{w_{t-1}}=(r,c)$ and $\mathbf{x}=(i,w_{t-1}(i))\in{\sf Piv}(\mathbf{z}_{w_{t-1}})$ . By (T.2), if $(r,c^{\prime})\in D({w_{t-1}})$ is in the same connected component as $\mathbf{z}_{w_{t-1}}$ , the move $i$ takes $(r,c^{\prime})$ strictly north of row $r$ . Thus, each march move strictly reduces the number of components in row $r$ . Let $t_{0}=\min\{t\in I^{(r)}\}$ . Since there are at most $r$ $\bullet$ ’s weakly above row $r$ , $D(w_{t_{0}})$ has at most $r-1$ (non-dominant) components in row $r$ . Hence (30) holds, as desired. ∎

#### Proposition 5.13.

Let $v$ be vexillary with ${\sf code}(v)=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{L^{\prime}})$ and $L^{\prime}\leq L$ . There exists an $O(L^{2})$ -time algorithm to check if $R=(r_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq L^{\prime}}$ is $R=R(T)$ for some $T\in{\sf SSYT}(\lambda(v),\phi(v))$ .

#### Proof.

Since $L^{\prime}\leq L$ , it is $O(L^{2})$ -time to calculate $\phi(v),\lambda(v)$ . Let

$$ \lambda_{i}:=\sum_{j=1}^{L^{\prime}}r_{ij},\text{\ for $1\leq i\leq L^{\prime}$.} $$

First verify (in $O(L)$ -time) that $\lambda_{i}\geq\lambda_{i+1}$ for $1\leq i\leq L^{\prime}-1$ . Then $R=R(T)$ where $T$ is the (unique) row weakly increasing tableau of shape $\lambda$ with $r_{ij}$ many $j$ ’s in row $i$ .

To verify $T\in{\sf SSYT}(\lambda(v),\phi(v))$ we must check that it is (i) is flagged by $\phi(v)$ , (ii) has shape $\lambda(v)$ , and (iii) is semistandard. For (i), we need

$$ r_{ij}=0\mbox{ if }j>\phi(v)_{i},\mbox{ for all }i,j\in[L^{\prime}]. $$

For (ii), we need

$$ \lambda_{i}=\lambda(v)_{i}\mbox{ for each }i\in[L^{\prime}]. $$

For (iii), it remains to ensure that $T$ is column strict, i.e.,

$$ \sum_{j^{\prime}\leq j}r_{i+1,j^{\prime}}\leq\sum_{j^{\prime}<j}r_{i,j^{\prime}}\mbox{ for each }i\in[L^{\prime}-1],j\in[L^{\prime}]. $$

We found the inequalities (32) and (33) from a (preprint) version of [12]. The inequalities (31), (32), and (33) can be checked in $O(L^{2})$ -time since $i,j\in[L^{\prime}]\subseteq[L]$ . ∎

The following completes our proof that we can check that $(S,R)\in X_{\alpha,w}$ in $L^{O(1)}$ -time.

#### Proposition 5.14.

Given $(S,R)\in X$ and $({\sf code}(w),\alpha)$ , one can determine if $(S,R)\in X_{\alpha,w}$ in $L^{O(1)}$ -time.

#### Proof.

By Propositions 5.11 and 5.12 combined, one determines in $O(L^{4})$ -time if $S$ encodes a path $w:=w_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}w_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\cdots\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s_{h}}}{{\longrightarrow}}w_{h}=v$ in $\mathcal{T}(w)$ . If so, the length of ${\sf code}(v)$ is at most $L$ . Thus, using Theorem 5.1, one checks $v$ is vexillary in $O(L^{3})$ -time. This decides if $S$ satisfies (X.1’). Proposition 5.13 checks $R$ satisfies (X.2’) in $O(L^{2})$ -time. Finally since $h\leq L^{2}$ , computing ${\sf delwt}(S)$ takes $O(L^{2})$ -time. Hence (X.3’) is checkable in $O(L^{2})$ time. ∎

Proof of Theorem 5.6: By Proposition 5.9, $\#X_{\alpha,w}=c_{\alpha,w}$ . By Proposition 5.12, $(S,R)\in\#X_{\alpha,w}$ only if the list $S$ has at most $L^{2}$ elements. Assuming this, we check $(S,R)$ satisfies (X.1) and (X.2) in $O(L^{2})$ -time. Using Proposition 5.14, we can verify $(S,R)\in X_{\alpha,w}$ in $L^{O(1)}$ -time. Thus, given input $\alpha$ and ${\sf code}(w)$ , computing $c_{\alpha,w}$ is in $\#{\sf P}$ . ∎

### 5.4. Hardness, and the conclusion of the proof of Theorem 1.5

Schur polynomials are an important basis of the vector space of symmetric polynomials. The Schur polynomial $s_{\lambda}=a_{\lambda+\delta}/a_{\delta}\text{ \ \ where $\lambda=(\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{n}\geq 0)$, $a_{\gamma}:=\det(x_{i}^{\gamma_{j}})_{i,j=1}^{n}$}$ , and $\delta=(n-1,n-2,\ldots,2,1,0)$ . The flagged Schur function of Section 5.1 is a generalization of the Schur polynomial.

A permutation $w$ is grassmannian if it has at most one descent $i$ , i.e., where $w(i)>w(i+1)$ . Given a partition $(\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{L}\geq 0)$ define a grassmannian permutation $w_{\lambda}$ by setting

$$ w_{\lambda}(i)=i+\lambda_{L-i+1}\text{\ for $1\leq i\leq L$.} $$

For $w_{\lambda}$ grassmannian, it is well-known (see, e.g., [10]) that

$$ {\sf code}(w_{\lambda})=(\lambda_{L},\lambda_{L-1},\ldots,\lambda_{1}). $$

Moreover,

$$ {\mathfrak{S}}_{w_{\lambda}}=s_{\lambda}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L})=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{L}}K_{\lambda,\alpha}x^{\alpha}, $$

where $K_{\lambda,\alpha}$ is the Kostka coefficient. This number counts semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda$ with content $\alpha$ .

By (35),

$$ c_{\alpha,w_{\lambda}}=K_{\lambda,\alpha}. $$

By Theorem 5.6, counting $c_{\alpha,w}$ is in $\#{\sf P}$ . Suppose there is an oracle to compute $c_{\alpha,w}$ in polynomial time in the input length of $({\sf code}(w),\alpha)$ . This input length is the same as for the input $\lambda,\alpha$ for $K_{\lambda,\alpha}$ . Hence (34) and (36) combined imply a polynomial-time counting reduction from $\{c_{\alpha,w}\}$ to Kostka coefficients. Now H. Narayanan [12] proved that counting $K_{\lambda,\alpha}$ is a $\#{\sf P}$ -complete problem. Thus counting $c_{\alpha,w}$ is a $\#{\sf P}$ -complete problem. ∎

#### Remark 5.15.

Suppose the input for counting $c_{\alpha,w}$ is $(\alpha,w)$ where $w\in S_{n}$ (in one-line notation). Then the above counting reduction is not polynomial time in the input length of the Kostka problem. For example, suppose $\lambda=\alpha=(2^{L},2^{L},\ldots,2^{L})$ ( $L$ -many). Then the input length of this instance of the Kostka problem is $2L^{2}\in O(L^{2})$ . On the other hand, $w_{\lambda}\in S_{L+2^{L}}$ . Therefore, a polynomial time algorithm for the Schubert coefficient problem in $n$ would have $\Omega(2^{L})$ run time for the Kostka problem.

It seems unlikely that there is a polynomial-time reduction under this input assumption. This is our justification to encode $w$ via ${\sf code}(w)$ rather than one line notation. ∎
